why:
A molecule is linear only when the electron pairs around its central atom are arranged so that the two bonded atoms sit at \(180^\circ\).

In \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) the carbon atom carries two \(\sigma\)-bonded regions and no lone pair, which is the two-electron-pair case of Table 5.3 — arrangement linear, molecular geometry linear. Table 5.4 prints \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) with its bond angle marked \(180^\circ\), and Table 5.8 lists its geometry as linear with \(\mu = 0\). So \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) is the linear molecule.

The other three are not:

\(\mathrm{SO_3}\) — the central sulphur has three bonded regions and no lone pair, the three-electron-pair case of Table 5.3, which is trigonal planar (the same shape the chapter gives \(\mathrm{BF_3}\) and \(\mathrm{BCl_3}\)), not linear.

\(\mathrm{H_2S}\) — two bonded pairs and two lone pairs on sulphur. That is the \(\mathrm{AB_2E_2}\) type of Table 5.4, whose shape is bent, and \(\mathrm{H_2S}\) is named there explicitly; Table 5.8 also gives its geometry as bent.

\(\mathrm{Cl_2O}\) — the central oxygen likewise has two bonded pairs and two lone pairs, again \(\mathrm{AB_2E_2}\), so it is bent for exactly the reason \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) and \(\mathrm{OF_2}\) are.

Hence the linear molecule among the four is carbon dioxide.

The three interactions named are of quite different kinds. A covalent bond is a genuine chemical bond formed by sharing an electron pair; a hydrogen bond and a van der Waals interaction are intermolecular attractions, and a hydrogen bond — an attraction to a hydrogen already bonded to a strongly electronegative atom — is the stronger of those two. So the decreasing order of strength is covalent, then hydrogen, then van der Waals.

The chapter's own Table 5.6 supports the first step of that order directly: the average bond enthalpies of ordinary covalent bonds run from about \(175\) to \(854\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\), an energy far larger than any intermolecular attraction, so a covalent bond must head the list.

Each of the other three options places something above the covalent bond or swaps the two intermolecular forces: one puts van der Waals above hydrogen bonding, one puts hydrogen bonding above the covalent bond, and one reverses the correct order completely. All three are therefore wrong.

The option that reads "covalent > hydrogen > van der Waals" is the correct order. Note that this chapter deals only with ionic, covalent and co-ordinate bonding — it does not itself develop hydrogen bonding or van der Waals forces, so the relative ranking of those two comes from general knowledge of intermolecular forces rather than from any statement in this chapter. Option (a) is also printed with the misprint "covalcnt".

Section 5.3 introduces the valence shell electron pair repulsion theory as "one of the popular models used earlier to predict the shapes of covalent molecules". Its whole apparatus — counting bonded pairs and lone pairs on the central atom, and letting them arrange themselves so that repulsion is minimum — produces a geometry, and Tables 5.3 and 5.4 use it to assign shapes such as linear, trigonal planar, bent, trigonal pyramidal and square planar to molecules and ions. So what VSEPR predicts is the shapes of molecules and ions.

Energy levels in an atom are a result of the quantum mechanical model of the atom; VSEPR neither calculates nor uses them.

Electronegativity is a periodic property of an element. VSEPR makes no statement about it — indeed the chapter uses electronegativity separately, in §5.6.5, to decide bond polarity, not shape.

The type of bonding in a compound is decided before VSEPR is applied at all: VSEPR starts from a Lewis diagram in which the bonds have already been drawn, and §5.6.5 shows that whether a bond is ionic, polar covalent or non-polar covalent follows from the electronegativity difference.

Hence VSEPR is used to predict the shapes of molecules and ions.

Two separate questions are being asked — is the bond polar, and is the molecule polar — and for \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) the answers differ.

The bond. Section 5.6.5 states that when a covalent bond joins atoms of different electronegativity the shared pair is pulled towards the more electronegative atom, separating charge and producing a dipole. Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so each \(\mathrm{C=O}\) bond carries a dipole and is polar.

The molecule. The dipole moment of a polyatomic molecule is the vector sum of its individual bond dipoles, so it depends on the shape. \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) is linear (Table 5.3 and Table 5.8), so its two \(\mathrm{C=O}\) dipoles are equal in magnitude and point in exactly opposite directions; they cancel and the resultant is zero. This is the same argument the chapter applies to \(\mathrm{BeF_2}\), and Table 5.8 records \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) with \(\mu = 0\ \mathrm{D}\). The molecule is therefore non-polar.

The two options that call the \(\mathrm{C=O}\) bond non-polar are ruled out at once, since carbon and oxygen have different electronegativities. The remaining rival calls both the bond and the molecule polar, which would require a non-zero dipole moment and contradicts the \(\mu = 0\) entry for \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) in Table 5.8.

So the true statement is: the \(\mathrm{C=O}\) bond is polar while the \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) molecule is non-polar.

The paramagnetism of oxygen is the standard case in which molecular orbital theory succeeds where the earlier models fail.

Section 5.5.4 states that a molecule with at least one half-filled molecular orbital is paramagnetic. Filling the molecular orbitals of \(\mathrm{O_2}\) (16 electrons) gives \((\sigma 1s)^2 (\sigma^* 1s)^2 (\sigma 2s)^2 (\sigma^* 2s)^2 (\sigma 2p_z)^2 (\pi 2p_x)^2 (\pi 2p_y)^2 (\pi^* 2p_x)^1 (\pi^* 2p_y)^1\), and the chapter says in so many words that \(\mathrm{O_2}\) is paramagnetic because of the two unpaired electrons in the \(\pi^*\) orbitals. Only MO theory produces that configuration.

Valence bond theory is explicitly ruled out by the chapter itself: limitation (ii) in §5.4.7 says oxygen is expected to be diamagnetic on VBT, that VBT leaves no unpaired electrons, and that "this theory fails to explain paramagnetism of oxygen molecule".

Hybridization is a device within valence bond theory for explaining shapes and equivalent bonds; it says nothing about electron spin, and no hybridization is invoked for a homonuclear diatomic such as \(\mathrm{O_2}\).

VSEPR predicts the geometry of a molecule from the repulsion of electron pairs; it makes no statement about magnetic behaviour at all, and \(\mathrm{O_2}\) is diatomic and so linear whatever its magnetism.

Hence the paramagnetism of \(\mathrm{O_2}\) is explained on the basis of molecular orbital theory.

Compare the four bond angles the chapter gives.

\(\mathrm{CH_4}\) — carbon is \(sp^3\) hybridized with no lone pair, so the four bonds point at the corners of a regular tetrahedron and the H-C-H angle is \(109^\circ 28'\) (§5.4.5).

\(\mathrm{C_2H_2}\) — each carbon is \(sp\) hybridized, and §5.4.5 states that the two \(sp\) hybrid orbitals lie at \(180^\circ\) to each other, so this is the largest angle of the four, not the smallest.

\(\mathrm{NH_3}\) — nitrogen is \(sp^3\) hybridized with one lone pair. The lone pair-bond pair repulsion pushes the bonded pairs together and the angle falls from the tetrahedral value to about \(107^\circ\) (Table 5.5).

\(\mathrm{H_2O}\) — oxygen is \(sp^3\) hybridized with two lone pairs. Two lone pairs squeeze the bonded pairs harder than one does, so the angle falls further still, to about \(104^\circ\) (§5.3 gives \(104^\circ 35'\), Table 5.5 gives \(104^\circ 28'\)).

The values therefore run \(180^\circ > 109^\circ 28' > 107^\circ > 104^\circ\), so the angle between two covalent bonds is minimum in the water molecule.
